source_text: Sed iudicat plane malum nolendo et damnat prohibendo, dimittit autem non uindicando et absoluit non puniendo. o deum ueritatis praeuaricatorem, sententiae suae circumscriptorem! timet damnare quod damnat. timet odisse quod non amat, factum sinit quod fieri non sinit, mauult ostendere quid nolit quam probare. hoc erit bonitas imaginaria, disciplina phantasma et ipsa, transfunctoria praecepta, secura delicta. audite, peccatores, quique nondum hoc estis, ut esse possitis:\' deus melior inuentus est, qui nec offenditur nec irascitur nec ulciscitur, cui nullus ignis coquitur in gehenna, cui nullus dentium frendor horret in exterioribus tenebris: bonus tantum est. denique prohibet delinquere, sed litteris solis. in uobis est, si uelitis illi obsequium subsignare. ut honorem deo habuisse uideamini; timorem enim non uult atque adeo prae se ferunt Marcionitae, quod deum suum omnino non timeant. \'malus enim\', inquiunt, \'timebitur, bonus autem diligetur\', stulte, quem dominum appellas negas timendum, cum hoc nomen potestatis sit, etiam timendae? at quomodo diliges, nisi timeas non diligere? plane nec pater tuus est, in quem competat et amor propter pietatem et timor propter potestatem, nec legitimus dominus, ut diligas propter humanitatem et timeas propter disciplinam. sic denique plagiarii diliguntur, non etiam timentur. non enim timebitur nisi iusta et ordinaria dominatio. diligi autem potest etiam adultera; sollicitatione enim con-, stat, non auctoritate, et adulatione. non potestate. quid denique adulantius quam delicta non exequi? age itaque, qui deum non times quasi bonum, quid non in omnem libidinem ebullis, summum, quod sciam, fructum uitae omnibus, qui deum non timent? quid non frequentas tam sollemnes uoluptates circi furentis et caueae saeuientis et scaenae lasciuientis? quid non et in persecutionibus statim oblata acerra animam negatione lucraris? absit, inquis, absit! ergo iam times delictum et timendo probasti illum timeri, qui prohibet delictum. aliud est, si eadem dei tui peruersitate quae non times obseruas, qua et ille quod non uindicat prohibet. — multo adhuc uanius, cum interrogati: quid fiet peccatori cuique die illo? respondent abici illum. qua? si ab oculis, nonne et hoc iudicio agitur? iudicatur enim abiciendus, et utique iudicio damnationis; nisi si in salutem abicitur peccator, ut et hoc deo optimo competat. et quid erit abici, nisi amittere id, quod erat consecuturus. si non abiceretur, id est salutem? ergo salutis in detrimentum abicietur, et hoc decerni non poterit nisi ab irato et offenso et executore delicti, id est iudice.
pass_a_gloss: But He judges evil plainly by not willing and condemns by forbidding, however He dismisses by not avenging and absolves by not punishing. Oh God, transgressor of truth, circumscriber of His own sentence! He fears to condemn what He condemns. He fears to hate what He does not love, He allows the deed which He does not allow to be done, He prefers to show what He does not will rather than to prove. This will be imaginary goodness, phantom discipline, and transitory precepts, secure offenses. Hear, sinners, and you who are not yet, so that you may be able to be: a better God has been found, who is neither offended nor angered nor avenged, for whom no fire is prepared in Gehenna, for whom no gnashing of teeth is feared in outer darkness: He is good only. Finally, He forbids sinning, but only by letters. It is in you, if you wish to subscribe to His service, so that you may seem to have honor for God; for He does not want fear, and therefore the Marcionites bring forth that they do not fear their God at all. For they say, 'The evil one will be feared, but the good one will be loved', foolishly, since you deny that the Lord you call is to be feared, when this name is of power, even to be feared? But how will you love, unless you fear not to love? Clearly, neither is He your Father, with whom there is fitting both love because of piety and fear because of power, nor a legitimate Lord, so that you may love because of humanity and fear because of discipline. Thus, finally, favorite slaves are loved, but not also feared. For only a just and orderly dominion will be feared. But even an adulteress can be loved; for she is consistent with solicitation, not authority, and with adulation, not power. What, finally, is more adulterous than not to punish offenses? Come now, you who do not fear God as if He is good, what do you not rush into in every lust, the greatest, as I know, fruit of life for all who do not fear God? What do you not frequent, such solemn pleasures of the raging circus and the savage cave and the lascivious stage? What do you not even gain by immediately offering a censer and denying your soul in persecutions? Away with it, you say, away! Therefore, you already fear sin and, by fearing, you have proven that He who forbids sin is to be feared. It is different, if you observe the same perversity of your God, which you do not fear, by which He also forbids what He does not avenge. Much more vainly, when asked: what will happen to each sinner on that day? they respond: He will be cast away. How? If from sight, is this not also judged? For He is judged to be cast away, and certainly by a judgment of condemnation; unless the sinner is cast away for salvation, so that this also may be fitting for the best God. And what will it be to cast away, if not to lose what he was going to attain? If he is not cast away, that is, salvation? Therefore, he will be cast away to the detriment of salvation, and this cannot be decreed except by an angry and offended and avenging judge, that is, a judge.
pass_b_english: God judges evil outright by refusing to will it, condemns it by forbidding it — yet He dismisses the charge by refusing to avenge, and acquits by refusing to punish. Oh, God the truth-breaker, the self-imposed limiter of His own sentence! He shrinks from condemning what He condemns. He shrinks from hating what He does not love. He permits the very deed He forbids, preferring to display what He rejects rather than prove His case. The result: a make-believe goodness, a phantom discipline, precepts that expire, offenses left perfectly safe.

Listen, sinners — and you who have not yet become such, so that you may stay that way: a 'better' God has been discovered. He takes no offense, feels no anger, exacts no vengeance. No fire awaits in Gehenna for Him, no gnashing of teeth in outer darkness. He is simply good. He forbids sin, yes — but only on paper. Whether you enlist in His service is entirely up to you, so you can appear to honor God; He does not want your fear. That is why the Marcionites boast they do not fear their God at all.

They say, 'The evil one is feared, the good one is loved' — foolishly denying that the Lord they name is to be feared, when that very title means power, power that demands fear. How can you love unless you fear failing to love? Clearly He is not your Father, in whom both love from piety and fear from power belong together. Nor is He a legitimate Lord, so that you love Him for His humanity and fear Him for His discipline. In the end, favorites are loved but not feared. Only a just and orderly rule commands fear. Even an adulteress can be loved — she wins by seduction, not authority; by flattery, not power. What is more adulterous, finally, than leaving offenses unpunished?

So go ahead — you who do not fear God because He is 'good' — what lust will you not plunge into, the supreme fruit of life, as I know it, for all who do not fear God? What pleasure will you not frequent: the raging circus, the savage arena, the lascivious stage? In persecution, will you not instantly offer incense and buy your life by denying your soul? 'God forbid!' you cry. Then you already fear sin, and by fearing you have proved that the One who forbids sin is to be feared. Unless, of course, you follow the same perversity of your God — the one you do not fear — who forbids what He refuses to avenge.

Even more vainly, when asked what will become of each sinner on that day, they answer: he will be cast away. Cast away how? From sight? Is that not itself a judgment? He is judged worthy of being cast away — and surely by a judgment of condemnation — unless the sinner is cast away for salvation, so that this too might suit the 'best' God. What does 'cast away' mean, if not losing what he was about to gain? If he is not cast away, that is salvation? Then he is cast away to salvation's loss, and such a decree can come only from an angry, offended, avenging judge — that is, a judge.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex rhetorical structure of Tertullian's argument. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the theological nuances (e.g., 'truth-breaker' for 'praeuaricatorem', 'power that demands fear' for 'nomen potestatis, etiam timendae'). All scripture-alluded concepts (Gehenna, outer darkness, gnashing of teeth) are correctly handled. The distinction between 'love' and 'fear' as components of 'pietas' and 'disciplina' is preserved.
